title: Baker McKenzie deploys Legora, building on a decade of innovation
author: Legora

dom.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training

st.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training
st.an: The source accepts the platform-led rollout model but materially develops it by specifying how adoption should be implemented: client-value use cases, advanced lawyer training, dedicated Practice Innovation Lawyers, and joint workflow development between Legora’s legal engineers and the firm’s specialists. It supports deployment and anticipated scalability, while reporting no measured productivity, accuracy or client-outcome gains.
qs: "Our AI strategy is rooted in delivering better client outcomes, not technology for its own sake.

Legora's legal engineers will work directly alongside this team and the Practice Innovation Lawyers, helping to design, build, and iterate on custom workflows within the platform, accelerating the Firm's ability to turn legal expertise into scalable, repeatable solutions.

kp.k: Legora is rolling out across Baker McKenzie globally
kp.d: The press release announces that Baker McKenzie is making Legora available to lawyers throughout its global network. It presents the deployment as part of the firm’s longer-term innovation strategy, but provides no adoption figures, performance measurements, client-outcome data or implementation timetable beyond the May 12, 2026 announcement.
qs: Leading global law firm Baker McKenzie today announced a rollout of Legora, making the platform available to lawyers across its global network.
The announcement marks the latest milestone in the Firm’s sustained, decade-long commitment to innovating to deliver better client outcomes.

kp.k: The firm traces its AI strategy to 2016
kp.d: Baker McKenzie describes a staged institutional AI history: initial industry engagement in 2016, an AI strategy in 2017 and creation of an AI-first legal practice in 2021. These are the firm’s own historical claims in the press release rather than independently substantiated comparative findings.
qs: Baker McKenzie's AI journey began in 2016, when the Firm first positioned itself at the forefront of thinking about AI and machine learning in the legal industry.

The Firm was one of the first global law firms to put in place an AI strategy in 2017 and also one of the first to establish an AI-first legal practice in 2021 (then called BakerML, now called Applied AI).

kp.k: AI adoption is framed around better client outcomes
kp.d: Chief Innovation Officer Ben Allgrove says the firm evaluates AI by whether it increases the value of legal services for clients, rather than adopting technology for its own sake. He also argues that effective deployment requires technology partners to understand the firm’s clients and working practices and to develop solutions collaboratively.
qs: Our AI strategy is rooted in delivering better client outcomes, not technology for its own sake. We actively push back against the hype. We are looking for use cases where the deployment of AI, and other innovation, makes the product we sell more valuable for our clients,” said Ben Allgrove, Partner and Chief Innovation Officer at Baker McKenzie.

That requires more than software. It requires technology partners willing to build and learn alongside us, understand what our clients need and how we work, and then help us get to outcomes that actually deliver better.
We’re thrilled to have entered into this strategic partnership with Legora.

kp.k: AI proficiency is becoming a core lawyer capability
kp.d: Allgrove characterises effective AI use as part of being a high-performing lawyer in 2026, alongside legal knowledge. The firm says it is supporting this shift through firmwide training and an intensive, in-person AI Accelerator Program for selected associates and counsel across practice groups.
qs: Baker McKenzie is investing heavily in giving its lawyers the AI tools and training they need to ‘do law’ faster and better.
“Being a high-performing lawyer in 2026 is no longer just about knowing the law; it is about using AI effectively to deliver it,” added Ben Allgrove.

In addition to Legora, and other technology, the Firm is investing in advanced training, including a flagship AI Accelerator Program, which is an intensive, in-person program for high-performing associates and counsel across practice groups.

This is layered on top of the Firm’s global training program available to all lawyers and the recruitment of a new senior role, Practice Innovation Lawyer, in each of the Firm’s global practice groups.

kp.k: New innovation roles are embedded within practice groups
kp.d: The firm reports recruiting a Practice Innovation Lawyer for each global practice group, indicating a formal role dedicated to integrating innovation into legal practice. The document does not specify whether these positions are lawyer or non-lawyer roles, their reporting lines, or their effects on conventional staffing and leverage.
qs: This is layered on top of the Firm’s global training program available to all lawyers and the recruitment of a new senior role, Practice Innovation Lawyer, in each of the Firm’s global practice groups.

kp.k: Cross-disciplinary teams build reusable AI-enabled legal workflows
kp.d: Baker McKenzie says its Applied AI practice combines technologists and specialist lawyers to design and deploy intelligent workflows across transactions, disputes, compliance and advisory matters. The stated model turns legal expertise into scalable and repeatable solutions, although the release reports no quantified productivity, quality or financial results.
qs: Additionally, Baker McKenzie continues to invest in and grow its award-winning Applied AI practice – a cross-disciplinary team of technologists and specialist lawyers who design and deploy intelligent legal workflows across matters including large-scale transactions, disputes, global compliance audits, data breach response, transfer pricing, employment advice, and commercial projects.

Legora's legal engineers will work directly alongside this team and the Practice Innovation Lawyers, helping to design, build, and iterate on custom workflows within the platform, accelerating the Firm's ability to turn legal expertise into scalable, repeatable solutions.

kp.k: Legal engineers will collaborate directly with firm professionals
kp.d: The announced implementation model places Legora’s legal engineers alongside Baker McKenzie’s Applied AI team and Practice Innovation Lawyers. Their work is described as jointly designing, building and iterating custom platform workflows, making vendor personnel active collaborators in configuring legal-service delivery rather than merely supplying software.
qs: Legora's legal engineers will work directly alongside this team and the Practice Innovation Lawyers, helping to design, build, and iterate on custom workflows within the platform, accelerating the Firm's ability to turn legal expertise into scalable, repeatable solutions.

kp.k: Legora portrays deployment as sustained strategy execution
kp.d: Legora CEO and co-founder Max Junestrand characterises Baker McKenzie’s deployment as the culmination of a decade-long AI commitment rather than trend-following. This is the vendor executive’s assessment within a joint promotional press release, not independent evidence of comparative industry leadership or client impact.
qs: Baker McKenzie has one of the most serious and sustained commitments to AI in the legal industry,” said Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-Founder of Legora.
This is a firm that has been building toward this moment for a decade – not chasing a trend, but executing a strategy.
We are proud to be part of that next chapter, and to support their lawyers in delivering exceptional outcomes for clients around the world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The release presents AI as a means to improve lawyers’ speed and client outcomes, while Ben Allgrove makes effective AI use part of professional competence in 2026.
pts.d: Legora’s press release announces that Baker McKenzie is making Legora available across its global network and investing in tools and training so lawyers can work faster and better. Baker McKenzie Partner and Chief Innovation Officer Ben Allgrove describes greater client value as the purpose of adoption, rather than adoption for its own sake. He asserts that high-performing lawyers now need effective AI use as well as legal knowledge. These are stated objectives and a claim about professional expectations, not reported measurements of improvements already achieved.

pts.k: The release predicts that collaboration between legal engineers, specialist lawyers and innovation lawyers will accelerate the conversion of legal expertise into scalable, repeatable workflows.
pts.d: The release describes Baker McKenzie’s Applied AI practice as already designing and deploying intelligent legal workflows across transactions, disputes, compliance audits, data breach response, transfer pricing, employment advice and commercial projects. It says Legora’s legal engineers will collaborate with that team and Practice Innovation Lawyers to develop custom platform workflows. This is a lawyer-supported workflow model; the release does not claim autonomous replacement of lawyers or predict staffing reductions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is institutional experience, described implementation investments and executive statements, rather than quantified performance results.
pts.d: The release supports its account with Baker McKenzie’s reported AI history: initial work in 2016, an AI strategy in 2017 and an AI-first practice established in 2021. It also describes an existing Applied AI team, training programs and recruitment of practice-level innovation lawyers. Allgrove supplies the firm’s rationale, and Legora CEO and Co-Founder Max Junestrand endorses its sustained commitment. No benchmarks, measured time savings, quality comparisons or specific client-outcome results are supplied to demonstrate the anticipated benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The rollout is announced on May 12, 2026; effective AI use is framed as a current requirement, while workflow acceleration is prospective and depends on more than software.
pts.d: The release positions the rollout as the latest stage of a decade-long strategy. Allgrove explicitly dates his professional-performance claim to 2026. The legal-engineering collaboration is described in future terms without a completion date or quantified target. Allgrove conditions improved outcomes on selecting valuable use cases and working with technology partners who understand client needs and legal working practices. Training and specialist roles are presented as accompanying investments.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries and participants are Baker McKenzie’s global lawyers and clients, with specialist training and workflow-building responsibilities for particular roles.
pts.d: Lawyers across the firm’s network receive platform availability and access to global training. High-performing associates and counsel are the target of the intensive AI Accelerator Program. Each global practice group is to have a newly recruited senior Practice Innovation Lawyer. The Applied AI practice and Legora’s legal engineers collaborate on workflow development. Clients worldwide are the intended beneficiaries of faster, better and more valuable legal services. The release makes no specific claim about public access to justice, market-wide pricing or displacement of entry-level lawyers.
